 Social Security Is Changing in 2027 - 6 Updates Retirees Should Know Before January
 Some changes happen automatically, but others need your attention before January
 By
 Josh Koebert 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Nov. 11, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
Social Security is getting its annual tune-up for 2027, and this year's changes touch nearly every part of the program: benefit amounts, work rules, taxes, and the notices that explain it all. The Social Security Administration (SSA) confirmed the details in an October 2026 announcement, giving beneficiaries a window to review their accounts before the new figures take effect. 
Most of these updates happen automatically. But a few require you to check your my Social Security account, update your expected earnings, or simply read the fine print on a notice you might otherwise set aside. Here's a practical, end-of-year checklist of what's changing and what to look at now, before January arrives, especially if you're living on just Social Security .

 A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment is coming, and it changes your check automatically
Social Security benefits and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments will rise by 3.6% starting in 2027, according to the SSA's October 2026 announcement. The cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation, and it's calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, as tracked by the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. 
On average, retirement benefits will rise by about $75 a month, according to the SSA. The agency's 2027 COLA fact sheet estimates the average monthly benefit for all retired workers will climb from $2,095 to $2,170 after the adjustment. Other benefit categories will see increases too: the average payment for an aged couple both receiving benefits is projected to rise from $3,238 to $3,355, and the average for a widowed mother with two children is projected to rise from $3,932 to $4,074, per SSA figures. 
This adjustment happens automatically. You don't need to apply for it or request it. SSI recipients will see their increased payments begin December 31, 2026, according to the SSA, since January 1 is a federal holiday. Social Security retirement, survivor, and disability beneficiaries will see the COLA reflected in benefits payable starting in January 2027. That first payment would follow your usual schedule: Wednesday, January 13, if your birthday falls on the 1st through the 10th; January 20 for the 11th through the 20th; and January 27 for the 21st through the 31st. 
If you started receiving benefits before May 1997 or get both Social Security and SSI, you're on a different schedule, so check SSA's 2027 payment calendar. Before then, it's worth logging into your my Social Security account to make sure your address and direct deposit details are current, since you can change both online.

 The maximum possible benefit is increasing, but check which figure applies to you
Benefit maximums are also increasing in 2027, but it's worth understanding which maximum applies to your situation. For a worker who claims at full retirement age (FRA, the age at which you qualify for 100% of your calculated benefit) in 2027, the maximum monthly benefit is $4,188, up from $4,152 in 2026, according to the SSA's COLA fact sheet. 
That's not the highest amount available, though. The true ceiling applies to workers who delay claiming until age 70, since benefits generally grow for each year you wait beyond full retirement age, up to that point. As of early November, the SSA hadn't published a 2027 age-70 maximum, so retirees weighing delayed claiming may want to check SSA's maximum-benefit page again once the 2027 figure is confirmed. 
Either way, these maximums only apply to people who earned at or above the taxable maximum in roughly 35 years of work . Most retirees receive far less, which is why comparing your own benefit estimate against the average, not the max, could give a more realistic picture. 
 Earnings limits are rising for people who work while collecting benefits
If you're collecting Social Security before reaching full retirement age and still working, the earnings test limits are going up in 2027. For people who are under full retirement age for the entire year, the SSA will withhold $1 in benefits for every $2 earned above $25,560 a year, up from $24,480 in 2026. 
For people reaching full retirement age sometime in 2027, a higher exempt amount applies: $67,920 for earnings in the months before the month you hit full retirement age, with $1 withheld for every $3 earned above that limit. Starting the month you reach full retirement age, there's no earnings limit, according to the SSA. 
This is one area where you do need to take action. The SSA adjusts your benefits based on what you told it you'd earn, so if you're still working and collecting benefits, it's worth letting the SSA know if you expect your 2027 earnings to be different. You can call the SSA at 1-800-772-1213 or visit a local office. An outdated earnings estimate could lead to either an unexpected benefit reduction or an overpayment that has to be repaid later.

Turning that pile into steady income, year after year, through good markets and bad, without ever running out.  Your COLA notice will show the exact math, and it's worth reading closely
Every year, the SSA sends a personalized COLA notice showing your new benefit amount, the effective date, and any deductions, including Medicare premiums. For 2027, the SSA says these notices will use a simplified, one-page format with plain, personalized language, spelling out exact dollar amounts. 
If you have a my Social Security account, you could view your 2027 COLA notice online starting in late November 2026, up to three weeks before a paper notice would arrive, according to the SSA. If you don't have an account yet, you'll need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see your notice online. Anyone who hasn't enrolled in paperless notices will get a paper notice by mail in December. 
This is worth checking carefully, not skimming. Your raw COLA increase and your actual deposit increase could differ once Medicare Part B premiums or other deductions are factored in. CMS hadn't announced the 2027 Part B premium as of early November. The standard premium for 2026 is $202.90, and the SSA says your 2027 premium amount will appear in your my Social Security Message Center starting in late November. 
Reviewing the notice as soon as it arrives, rather than being surprised in January, gives you time to adjust a budget if the net increase is smaller than the headline 3.6% suggests. 
 The taxable maximum is rising for workers still paying into the system
For people still working, the maximum amount of earnings subject to Social Security tax is increasing to $192,300 in 2027, up from $184,500 in 2026, according to the SSA. This change affects only workers who earn more than $184,500 and happens automatically through payroll withholding, but it's a useful figure for anyone estimating next year's take-home pay or running retirement projections, since earnings above this threshold aren't taxed for Social Security and don't count toward future benefit calculations. 
 Disability thresholds are adjusting too
For SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance) recipients, substantial gainful activity (SGA) thresholds, the earnings level the SSA uses to determine if a disability benefit recipient is working enough to no longer be considered disabled, are rising in 2027. The non-blind SGA threshold increases to $1,770 a month, up from $1,690, while the blind threshold rises to $2,950 a month, up from $2,830, according to the SSA. The trial work period threshold, the earnings level that counts as a trial work month for beneficiaries testing their ability to work, is increasing to $1,270 a month, up from $1,210. 
The maximum federal SSI payment is increasing as well, to $1,029 a month for an individual and $1,544 for a couple in 2027, up from $994 and $1,491 in 2026, according to the SSA. Your own SSI payment could be lower based on your income, living situation, and other factors, and some states add a supplement. These adjustments happen automatically, so no action is needed beyond reviewing your own notice once it arrives. 
If you receive SSDI and work, earning more than the SGA threshold doesn't automatically stop your benefits. During a nine-month trial work period, you could still get your full payment no matter how much you earn, according to the SSA. You're required to report your work activity, and it could help to ask the SSA how these rules apply to your situation. 
 Retirement News: Almost 80% of Americans fear a retirement age increase — here’s the real reason why 
 Bottom line
Most of what's changing in 2027 happens without any effort on your part: the COLA increase, the new taxable maximum, and the disability and SSI threshold adjustments all apply automatically. Where you do have homework is updating your expected earnings if you're working while collecting benefits, and actually reading your personalized COLA notice once it's available, since that's where you'll see your real, after-deduction increase. 
Setting a reminder to check your my Social Security account in late November, or watching the mail in December, is a simple way to stay ahead of these changes. For anyone weighing when to claim or how a higher earnings limit might affect their plans, SSA's online benefit estimator could help translate these new numbers into a personal plan. And if your raise doesn't go as far as you'd hoped, a few simple moves could help you stretch your retirement dollars further .
